en: So when creating a post, but also for many
other routes, we're reaching out to the
database here to start a transaction, which
simply means we have multiple steps which we
wanna perform in one go. And if one of them
fails, we wanna roll back all of them.
Now, not all post routes or routes in
general use transactions.
For example, for listing my posts, for
getting a list of all posts, I don't have a
transaction there, I just directly query my
database. But how exactly does this work?
Well, db
is a database object created with the
database class coming from Bun's SQLite
package.
Because this project here uses a SQLite
package stored in an app.sqlite file here,
and that's all set up in a connection.ts
file, which is in the source/db folder in
that API app project. Project.
So in there, I'm really just setting up my
SQLite database. Super simple here, enabling
WAL mode, which gives us better performance,
enforcing foreign key constraints so that we
get an error if we insert invalid foreign
keys.
And that is about it.
The database is stored in a path that's
coming from an environment variable, or we
use a default path if that's not set. So we
do support environment variables here for
the database path. And then in our actual
app logic, we use this database object with
the methods supported by the Bun SQLite
client to query the database, to get data,
or like in createPost, also to run a
transaction where we then also try to insert
some data, for example.
And we're using features like this query
parameters syntax supported by Bun to safely
insert dynamic values into our queries.
And then this query just gets executed by
calling the run method where the concrete
values are inserted for these placeholders.
And Bun's SQLite package does that in a way
that protects against SQL injection attacks,
for example.
And that's really all that's to that
database feature. The only other thing worth
noting is that we also import this database
into our auth.ts file
and there we link it to the database field
of the Batteroff package so that the
Batteroff package knows where to set up its
auth-related tables like the users table,
the sessions table, and so on. And the great
thing is that BetterAuth natively supports
Bun's SQLite package. So using Bun SQLite
with BetterAuth is a breeze.
